units.name: glob-matching
units.role: Compile shell-style glob patterns into matchers and test a path against one or many globs at once.
units.description: This is the project's expert on shell-style file patterns such as *.rs, src/**/foo.rs or {a,b}.txt. It takes such a pattern as a person wrote it, checks that it is well formed (reporting a clear complaint such as 'unclosed character class' if not), and translates it into an internal form a fast matching engine can run. It can also take a whole collection of patterns and prepare them so a single file path can be tested against all of them in one pass, reporting the position number of every pattern that matched, which is how the caller learns which specific rule applied. To stay fast on very large collections it sorts patterns into buckets by shape (a plain name, a name-only literal, a bare extension, a fixed prefix, a fixed suffix, everything else) so cheap checks handle most patterns and the general engine handles only the rest. It normalises Windows-style backslashes to forward slashes so a pattern behaves the same everywhere, and it can escape a piece of text so it is treated literally. It must never touch the disk, the network or the clock: it never checks whether a path exists, never reads a file, and never runs another program. It works purely on the text of the pattern and the text of the path it is handed, and the same pair must always give the same answer.

units.name: ignore-rules
units.role: Decide whether a path should be skipped, layering gitignore files, global git excludes, hidden-file rules, command-line globs and file-type selections in the right order of authority.
units.description: This part answers one question over and over: should this file or folder be looked at, or left alone? It reads the rule files people already keep in their projects (.gitignore, .ignore, .rgignore and a repository's private exclude file), plus the machine-wide rules git is configured with, plus rules given on the command line, plus a built-in table mapping names like 'rust' or 'python' to filename patterns. It then combines all of those in a strict order of authority: command-line rules beat rule files, rules closer to the file beat rules further up the tree, and an explicit keep-this can undo an earlier skip-this. It remembers the rules it has already read for each folder so a question about a nearby file can be answered without re-reading anything, and it offers a way to ask about a single path without scanning a whole tree at all. Its verdict is always one of three things: skip it, explicitly keep it, or no opinion. It must never look inside a file's contents, never decide what to search for, and never print anything; problems it hits while reading rule files are handed back to the caller rather than swallowed.

units.name: directory-walker
units.role: Enumerate files under one or more roots, single-threaded or across a work-stealing thread pool, applying ignore rules and depth, size, symlink and filesystem-boundary limits.
units.description: This is the file finder. Given one or more starting folders (or the special name meaning standard input), it walks through everything underneath them and hands back one item at a time: this file, that folder, or an error explaining why something could not be read. Before handing anything back it asks the ignore-rules part whether the item should be skipped, and it applies its own limits too: how deep to descend, how large a file may be, whether to follow shortcuts, whether to stay on a single disk, and whether to avoid the very file the program is writing its own output into. It offers two modes: a simple one-at-a-time list, and a parallel mode where several worker threads share the work by stealing from one another's queues and call a handler supplied by the caller, who can reply keep going, do not enter this folder, or stop everything. The same configuration object can also produce standalone path checkers that answer 'would this path be ignored?' without walking anything. It must never read a file's contents or decide what counts as a match; it only locates candidates. It must never silently swallow an error either — problems are surfaced as entries in the stream — and it must never descend past the limits it was given.

units.name: matcher-interface
units.role: Define the engine-agnostic contract for finding matches in bytes, exposing capture groups, and expanding replacement templates.
units.description: This is the shared rulebook every search engine inside the project must follow. It says what it means to find the next match starting at some position in a chunk of bytes, how a match is described (a start and an end position within that chunk), how the pieces captured inside a match are numbered and named, and how a replacement template such as 'Mr. $1' gets filled in with the captured text. It also carries a little shared vocabulary: what counts as a line ending (a single byte, or the two-byte Windows form), and a compact set of bytes that can never appear inside a match, which lets whole regions of a file be skipped. Because of this rulebook, the code that scans files and the code that prints results can be written once and work with either pattern engine without knowing which one it has. It is pure bookkeeping and arithmetic over byte ranges: it must never open files, touch the network, run programs, read the clock, or compile a pattern itself. It only describes the shape of the answer and leaves the real work to whichever engine implements it.

units.name: regex-matcher
units.role: Turn a user's pattern into a matcher backed by the built-in regex engine, rewriting it so it obeys line-oriented rules and extracting literals for fast prefiltering.
units.description: This takes the search pattern a person typed and turns it into something that can be run against the bytes of a file. Before compiling it, it rewrites the pattern according to the options in play: making it insensitive to capitalisation (including the 'smart' form, where capitals are ignored only if the user typed none), requiring matches to sit on word boundaries or to fill a whole line, treating the pattern as plain text rather than as a pattern, and honouring Windows line endings. Its most important job is line discipline: when the caller says lines end at a particular byte, it surgically removes that byte from every place the pattern could have matched it — for example, taking the newline out of 'any whitespace character' — so a reported match can never straddle two lines; and if the user literally asked for a newline, it refuses with a clear explanation rather than quietly changing what they asked for. It also refuses patterns containing a byte the caller has declared impossible, works out which bytes the pattern can never match so work can be skipped, and digs required literal text out of the pattern to build a cheap fast scan that finds candidate lines before the real, slower pattern runs. It must never report a match the real pattern would not report, and its fast scan must never miss a line the real pattern would have matched. It reads no files and contacts nothing.

units.description: This lets the program search using PCRE2, a long-established pattern-matching library written in C, instead of the built-in engine. Its job is to take the pattern the user typed plus the options they asked for — ignore capitalisation, smart capitalisation, whole word only, whole line only, treat the pattern as plain text, Unicode handling, multi-line behaviour, Windows line endings, and speed tuning such as compiling the pattern to machine code — hand them to the library in the form it expects, and then present the result through exactly the same small set of operations every other part of the program already knows: find the next match from a position, walk over all matches, count and name the parenthesised sub-parts, and record where each of them matched. It also joins several patterns into one and turns any failure from the underlying library into a single readable error. It must never read files, print anything, consult the environment, or decide what to search or how results are displayed; it only compiles patterns and reports match positions inside byte buffers it is handed. Because it depends on an outside library it is optional and can be left out of a build entirely, in which case asking for it produces a clear message rather than a crash.

units.role: Read content in bounded chunks, split it into lines, detect and handle binary data and character sets, run the matcher, and report every hit and context line to a caller-supplied receiver.
units.description: This is the part that actually performs a search over the contents of something — a file on disk, a stream such as piped input, or a block of bytes already in memory. It is handed two things by its caller: a way to test whether text matches, and a receiver that wants to be told about results. It then pulls the content in through a rolling window so that even enormous files never have to fit in memory at once, chops that content into lines, optionally converts text from other character sets into the standard one, guesses whether the content is binary rubbish (and either stops or scrubs it, depending on how it was configured), and walks line by line looking for matches. It can be told to do the opposite and report only lines that do not match, to include a fixed number of surrounding lines for context, to number lines, to allow a single match to span several lines, to stop after a given number of matches, and to cap how much memory it may use. For every match, every context line, every gap between context groups, and at the start and end of the whole search, it calls the receiver, and it obeys the receiver's request to stop early. It must never format or print output itself, never decide which files are worth searching, and never interpret the pattern — those belong elsewhere. It must never hold more than the configured amount of memory, and every read or configuration failure must be surfaced rather than swallowed.

units.name: result-printer
units.role: Render search results as the human-readable grep-style text, the terse count and file-list modes, and the running statistics.
units.description: This decides what a search result actually looks like when a person reads it. Given the raw hits handed back by the search machinery, it decides whether to show the file name, whether to put it on its own heading line, whether to prefix each line with a line number, a column number or a byte offset, how to separate one file's results from the next, how to present the extra lines of context around a hit, how to draw attention to the matched text, how to show substituted text when the user asked for a search-and-replace preview, how to trim leading whitespace, and what to do with an absurdly long line — truncate it, show a short preview, or say it was omitted. It also provides the terser modes: just a count per file, just the names of files that did or did not match, a silent mode that only records whether anything matched, and a plain list of paths for when the user only wants to know which files would be searched. Finally it keeps a running tally, per search and across searches, of how long things took and how many files, lines, bytes and individual matches were involved. It writes only to the destination its caller handed it, never opens files or contacts anything on its own, and must never change what counts as a match — only how a match is displayed.

units.name: json-output
units.role: Emit search results as a stream of machine-readable records, one per line, so other programs can consume them.
units.description: This reports what a search found in a form other programs can read rather than a form humans read. As the search machinery walks a file, it turns each event into one self-contained record on its own line: a begin record when a file starts being searched, a match record for every matching line carrying the line's text, its line number, its byte position in the file and the exact start and end of each matched piece (plus the substituted text if the user asked for one), a context record for the neighbouring lines shown around matches, and an end record with summary counts and how long the search took. Because searched files and even file names are not guaranteed to be valid text, it enforces a strict rule: anything that is valid text is written as an ordinary string, and anything that is not is written as encoded raw bytes under a different name, so nothing is ever silently mangled or lost. It must never invent, reorder, lossily convert or drop data, never prettify output for human eyes, never decide which files to search or how to match them, and never open a file itself — it only receives events and writes records to the stream it was handed.

units.name: terminal-styling
units.role: Parse colour specifications and clickable-link templates, and emit the terminal escape sequences that decorate printed output.
units.description: This handles the decoration of output for a terminal, as opposed to its layout. It has two jobs. First, it understands the small language users write for colour options — things like 'match:fg:red' or 'path:style:bold' — checks that each piece names a recognised target, attribute and value, explains clearly when it does not, and merges everything the user asked for together with sensible defaults into one settled set of styles for paths, line numbers, column numbers, matched text and highlighted lines. Second, it understands the template for clickable file links: it accepts either a hand-written template with placeholders for the path, line, column, machine name and compatibility-layer prefix, or one of a catalogue of built-in shortcuts named after popular editors, then checks the template begins with a proper address scheme and never uses a column placeholder without a line placeholder. For each printed file it fills the template in, converting the file's location into an absolute, properly-encoded address, and wraps the printed text in the sequence that makes it clickable. The machine name and compatibility prefix are handed to it by its caller; it never looks them up itself and never reads environment variables. It must not decide what gets printed or in what order, and must never emit escape sequences to a destination that has said it does not support them.

units.name: cli-io
units.role: Reusable command-line plumbing: terminal detection, buffered colour-capable output, pattern-file reading, byte escaping, size parsing and host name lookup.
units.description: This is the general-purpose toolbox a command-line program uses to talk to the terminal and to the user, without knowing anything about searching. It answers questions such as: is this program's input coming from a keyboard, or from a pipe or a file? Is its output going to a screen, or being redirected? Based on those answers it hands back an output channel that either flushes after every line, so a person watching the screen sees results immediately, or in large chunks, which is faster when writing to a file. It also reads a list of search patterns from a file or from piped input, one per line, reporting the exact file, line number and byte position when a line contains something that is not valid readable text. It converts awkward raw bytes into a printable form for error messages and converts such written forms back into raw bytes so users can type unprintable characters as arguments. It turns shorthand sizes like '2M' into an exact number of bytes with a friendly explanation when the input is malformed, and it asks the operating system for the machine's name. What it must never do is decide anything about searching, matching, filtering files or how results should look; it only supplies neutral utilities, and when something goes wrong it gives a clear explanation rather than crashing or hanging silently.

units.description: This lets the search look inside files it cannot read directly, by handing them to another program first. It keeps a table mapping file-name endings to the tool that can unpack them — names ending in one suffix go to one unpacker, another suffix to another — and it can also run any command the user nominates over every file before searching it. When a file needs such treatment it starts the helper, feeds it the file, and streams whatever the helper prints back out as if that were the file's real contents. It handles the fiddly, easy-to-get-wrong parts: it looks the helper up in the system's list of program directories and turns it into a full path, so a stray program sitting in the current folder can never be run by accident; it drains the helper's complaint channel on a separate thread so a chatty helper can never fill a buffer and freeze forever; and when the helper exits unhappily it reports exactly what the helper complained about rather than a vague failure. It must never silently swallow a helper's failure, never leave a started program running after the reader is done with it, and never decide what to search or how to match text — it only produces bytes for others to search. If no helper is known for a file, or the helper is not installed, it quietly falls back to reading the plain file.

units.description: This is the program's self-documentation department. The program keeps one master list describing every command-line option it accepts, including each option's short name, long name, negated form, sample value, one-line summary and full write-up. This unit walks that master list and renders it into the different formats people actually read: the terse one-screen summary, the long-form manual, the traditional manual page, and ready-to-install tab-completion scripts for four different shells. It also composes the version banners, which report the release number, the exact source revision it was built from, which processor acceleration features were compiled in and detected when it runs, and whether the optional alternative pattern engine is present. All of it is pure text assembly: it fills placeholders in stored templates and returns a finished string, leaving it to the caller to decide where that text is printed. It must never perform a search, read the user's files, write anything to disk, or decide what the program will do. And it must never drift out of step with the master option list — which is exactly why this text is generated from that list rather than written by hand.

units.description: This is the part responsible for talking to the person running the program about problems, as opposed to showing them search hits. It remembers three things for the whole run: whether ordinary complaints should be shown at all, whether complaints specifically about unreadable or malformed rule files should be shown, and whether anything has gone wrong so far. The first two switches are set once when the command line is read; the third is flipped on automatically whenever an error message is printed, so that when the program finishes it knows to report failure rather than success even though it kept going. It also supplies the standard way to print such a message: everything goes to the error channel, prefixed with the program's name, and while it is being written the normal output channel is held shut so a warning can never appear spliced into the middle of a line of results. If writing the message fails because the reader has gone away, the program quits quietly instead of complaining about complaining. Finally it holds the plumbing that carries the developer-facing running commentary requested by the debug and trace options, forwarding those notes to the same channel in the same interleave-safe way. It must never write to the results channel, never suppress or invent results, and never crash the program for an ordinary problem beyond setting that flag.

units.description: This is the program's command-line rulebook. It holds the master list of every option the program accepts — about a hundred and eighty of them — and for each one records its long name, its optional single-letter name, its aliases, an optional negative form that turns it back off, which documentation section it belongs to, its short and long help text, whether it takes a value, and exactly what changing that setting means. It also knows how to read an optional settings file whose location the user gives through an environment variable, treating each line of that file as though it had been typed on the command line before the real arguments. Given the words the user actually typed, it walks through them one at a time, matches each to a known option, complains about ones it does not recognise (suggesting near-miss spellings), demands a value where one is required, checks that the value is sensible, and records the result in a flat record with one slot per setting. It deliberately stops there: it must never actually do the work a setting implies — it does not open the files to be searched, does not build a search engine, does not run helper programs — and it short-circuits immediately when help or version output is requested, so those always work even when the rest of the settings are broken.

Once the command line has been read and every option recorded, this piece works out everything that could only be decided once all the options were known, and everything that depends on the surrounding environment: is output going to a screen or into a pipe, should colour be on, how many workers should run at once, was a target given or should the current folder — or whatever is being piped in — be searched, and which pattern text came from files rather than from arguments. It also encodes the small courtesies users expect, such as showing line numbers when a person is watching but not when output is being piped, or reporting one result per line when editor-friendly output is asked for. units.description: This is the part that actually is the command. Once the command line has been read and turned into a settled set of choices, it decides what job to do: search for a pattern, list the files that would be searched, list the known file types, print the manual page or a shell completion script, or build or consult an index. For a search it walks the requested folders — on one thread, or on many at once when order does not matter — and for each candidate decides whether it is even worth looking at: real files and anything the user named explicitly are searched, folders and stray shortcuts are skipped. For each file it then decides how to get at the text: read the file directly, which is fastest and can map it into memory; pipe it through a helper program the user nominated; transparently unpack it; or read piped input. It hands the content to the search machinery with the right formatter attached, tallies whether anything matched, optionally prints timing and counts at the end, and finally translates the whole run into the number the shell sees: zero if something matched, one if nothing did, two if something went wrong. It must never decide policy that belongs upstream — it does not read options or build patterns itself — never format match output on its own, and never treat a closed output pipe as a failure: when the reader goes away it stops quietly and reports success.

units.name: search-index
units.role: The experimental opt-in index: extract required short character sequences from a pattern, and own the on-disk database that maps those sequences to files.
units.description: This is the experimental, switched-off-by-default index. Normally the program finds things by walking every folder and reading every file. The idea here is to do some of that work ahead of time instead: scan the files once, break their contents into very short character sequences, and remember which files contained which sequences in a small database on disk. Later, when someone searches, the pattern itself is analysed to work out which sequences any possible match must contain, so the program can ask the database for a short list of candidate files rather than reading the whole tree. It has two halves: the library that owns the database — creating the storage folder, finding an existing one by looking in the current folder and each folder above it, or honouring a location named by an environment variable — and the analysis code that turns a pattern into a combination of required sequences joined by 'and' and 'or'. It also holds the small piece of wiring the main command calls, in two versions: a real one compiled in when the feature is switched on, and a stub that simply reports that indexing is not enabled in this build. It must never change the answers a search gives: it is only allowed to narrow down which files are worth looking at, never to decide on its own that something matched, and it must never take effect for users who did not ask for it. It is presently a prototype: the database is opened but never actually consulted, and the search still falls back to reading everything.

unpartitioned.reason: A pure facade: six re-export lines and a doc comment, with no logic of its own. It is the public library front door for six different units at once (command-line plumbing, the matcher contract, both pattern engines, the printers and the search engine), so it belongs to no single unit; assigning it to any one of them would misstate ownership.

violations_observed.note: The walker imports crate-private items (PartialErrorBuilder, dir::Ignore, dir::IgnoreBuilder, the incremental-matcher options) that are not part of the ignore crate's public API. They are listed as entrypoints so the edges resolve, but they are not a stable contract.
The walker drives the private per-folder matcher tree directly, so the walker — not the ignore code — decides when rule files are loaded.
The walker constructs errors using the module-private Error::with_path / with_depth / from_walkdir helpers defined in crates/ignore/src/lib.rs:263, 271, 287.

Reverse edge: the ignore code imports the walker's DirEntry type, so these two units are mutually recursive at the type level. Neither can be extracted from the other without moving DirEntry into a shared place.

The machine-readable printer reaches into crate-private internals of its sibling (the byte-counting writer, the replacer and the in-context match re-finder). The two are separable only as long as they stay in one crate.

The on-the-wire shape of the summary record's statistics object is defined by result-printer's serialization of Stats, not by json-output, so the machine-readable contract is not fully owned by the unit that publishes it.
This infra unit calls a crate-private number formatter owned by result-printer, while result-printer depends on this unit's link interpolator — a mutual dependency at the crate-internal level.

The printer crate root, owned by result-printer, is what re-exports the public surface of both json-output and terminal-styling; a change to either sibling's public API edits a file result-printer owns.

The crate root owned by cli-io is what declares and re-exports preprocessor-runner's modules and symbols, and its crate-level documentation describes them. Every outside caller reaches preprocessor-runner through a file this unit owns.

The module root owned by flag-parsing re-exports symbols that originate in its two siblings — HiArgs from arg-wiring and all ten generator functions from flag-docs — so those units' names are published by a file they do not own.

The wiring stage constructs the driver's crate-private types (SearchWorker, Printer, PatternMatcher, Haystack) while the driver calls back into HiArgs for nearly every decision. This is a genuine two-way dependency, permitted only because both live in one crate.

The wiring stage is not purely configuration: private helpers there read pattern files, probe standard input, guess the working directory, and shell out to an external program to get the machine name — behaviour that arguably belongs in cli-io rather than in an argument-resolution unit.

The driver hand-writes a summary record that deliberately mimics the machine-readable printer's format instead of going through it. Nothing enforces the match, so the two will drift if the record format changes.

The index seam is currently hollow: the enabled path opens the database, discards it, and delegates to the ordinary exhaustive search. No query ever reaches the database, and the n-gram analysis in crates/index/src/literal.rs has no caller outside its own tests, so the two halves of this unit are not yet connected to each other.
The index is actually discovered and constructed inside the wiring stage rather than inside this unit, which leaves the enabled/disabled shim as a very thin seam over logic that lives elsewhere.
